uncited: It differs from its siblings by focusing on uniform spatial distribution over mesh geometry for training data generation, rather than foot-point projection or edge-based sampling.
**Inputs:** A mesh defined by vertices and triangular faces.
**Outputs:** A list of 3D points on the surface.
Each row contains indices into `vertices`.
For each face in the surface, extract vertices $v_1, v_2, v_3$.
Generate two random numbers $a$ and $b$ between 0 and 1.
If $a + b > 1$, swap them: $a, b = 1 - a, 1 - b$.
Compute the point as a convex combination of the vertices: $point = a \cdot v_1 + b \cdot v_2 + c \cdot v_3$.
Repeat for the specified number of samples per face.
Degenerate triangles (zero area) will produce points along a line or point, which may bias the distribution if not filtered.
It differs from the base method by adding directional encoding for view and light vectors, enabling the neural network to learn view-dependent reflectance.
Choose this when training a NeRF-based reflectance model that requires explicit angular encoding of illumination and viewing geometry.
Compute camera difference vector $cam\_diff = camera\_position - point$.
Calculate $\theta_{cam}$: $\theta_{cam} = \text{degrees}(\arctan2(cam\_diff[1], cam\_diff[0]))$.
Calculate $\phi_{cam}$: $\phi_{cam} = \text{degrees}(\arctan2(cam\_diff[2], \sqrt{cam\_diff[0]^2 + cam\_diff[1]^2}))$.
Compute light difference vector $light\_diff = light.position - point$.
Calculate $\theta_{light}$: $\theta_{light} = \text{degrees}(\arctan2(light\_diff[1], light\_diff[0]))$.
Calculate $\phi_{light}$: $\phi_{light} = \text{degrees}(\arctan2(light\_diff[2], \sqrt{light\_diff[0]^2 + light\_diff[1]^2}))$.
Append the point, view directions $[\theta_{cam}, \phi_{cam}]$, light directions $[\theta_{light}, \phi_{light}]$, and color to their respective lists.
